blocks.text: The incense altar is positioned 'before the veil that is by the ark of the testimony' (v. 6), placing it within the graded sanctuary architecture. The tabernacle organizes access through curtains, veils, rooms, and furnishings, creating graduated levels of sacred space. Aaron's daily burning of incense (vv. 7-8) and annual atonement ritual (v. 10) are priestly duties tied to this spatial arrangement. Barriers and authorized personnel are not merely decorative but integral to the approach to holiness, structuring how Israel encounters the divine presence.

The census tax represents a distinct communal obligation. When Israel was counted, each adult male gave a half-shekel as a 'ransom for his soul' (v. 12). This payment expressed corporate responsibility for sanctuary worship and maintenance—distinguishable from gifts, vows, or foreign taxation. The uniformity of the contribution, regardless of wealth, underscores shared obligation to sustain sanctuary operations.

The half-shekel offering became a foundational scriptural precedent for temple revenue. By the Second Temple period, this levy had been institutionalized across diaspora communities and Judean centers, shaping how sanctuary support was collected and understood for centuries. The practice's continuity across generations reflects its establishment here in Exodus as divinely ordained.
